clinicalPearls: FTD is a group of clinical syndromes united by underlying frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) pathology; like other major neurodegenerative diseases it is considered a disorder of abnormal protein aggregation, with either tau or TDP-43 (transactive response DNA-binding protein of 43 kDa) implicated in most cases (Harrison 22e p.3485).
Younger onset than typical Alzheimer's: FTD most often begins in the fifth to seventh decades of life and is nearly as prevalent as Alzheimer's disease in this age group (Harrison 22e p.3485).

Three core clinical syndromes are described: the behavioral variant (bvFTD, the most common) and two forms of primary progressive aphasia (PPA) - the semantic and nonfluent/agrammatic variants (Harrison 22e p.3485-3486).

bvFTD manifests as social and emotional dysfunction - apathy, disinhibition, compulsivity, loss of empathy, and overeating - often but not always accompanied by deficits in executive control (Harrison 22e p.3486).

In semantic variant PPA patients slowly lose the ability to decode word, object, person-specific, and emotion meaning; in nonfluent/agrammatic variant PPA patients develop profound inability to produce words, often with prominent motor speech impairment (Harrison 22e p.3486).

Parietal functions such as visuospatial processing and arithmetic calculation are typically unaffected even late in the FTD syndromes, helping distinguish it from Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3486).

Any of the three syndromes, most often bvFTD, may be accompanied by motor neuron disease (MND), in which case the term FTD-MND is applied; corticobasal syndrome (CBS) and progressive supranuclear palsy-Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS) are also considered part of the FTD clinical spectrum (Harrison 22e p.3486).
In contrast to Alzheimer's disease, the cholinergic system is relatively spared in FTD, which accounts for the poor efficacy of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in this group (Harrison 22e p.3486).
Treatment is symptomatic only; there are currently no therapies known to slow progression or improve symptoms, and no disease-modifying treatments have shown efficacy to date (Harrison 22e p.3487).
harrison.pathophysiology: FTD is linked to frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), characterized by focal atrophy of frontal, insular, and/or temporal cortex; atrophy often begins focally in one hemisphere before spreading to anatomically interconnected cortical and subcortical regions. bvFTD shows medial/orbital frontal cortex and anterior insula degeneration, semantic variant PPA the anterior temporal region, and nonfluent/agrammatic PPA the opercular frontal and precentral gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. Microscopically there is gliosis, microvacuolation, and neuronal loss; the disease is subtyped by the protein composition of neuronal and glial inclusions, which contain either tau or TDP-43 in roughly 90% of patients, with the remaining ~10% showing inclusions containing the FET family of proteins (FUS, Ewing sarcoma protein, TAF-15). Loss of cortical serotonergic innervation is common while the cholinergic system is relatively spared. Misfolded proteins are increasingly recognized to have prion-like/corruptive templating properties that may drive network-rooted patterns of disease spread. Autosomal dominant inheritance is seen in only 10-20% of cases, with mutations in C9orf72 (the most common genetic cause, a noncoding GGGGCC hexanucleotide expansion, presenting as bvFTD with or without MND and overlapping with ALS), GRN/progranulin, and MAPT/tau (Harrison 22e p.3485-3487).
additionalDifferentials: Alzheimer's disease (FTD has relatively preserved memory and parietal function early; a small percentage of FTD syndromes show Alzheimer's pathology at autopsy) (Harrison 22e p.3486-3487)
Progressive supranuclear palsy-Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS) - within the FTD spectrum; falls, vertical supranuclear ophthalmoparesis, axial rigidity (Harrison 22e p.3487)
Corticobasal syndrome (CBS) - asymmetric rigidity, dystonia, myoclonus, apraxia, alien limb phenomena (Harrison 22e p.3488)
Idiopathic Parkinson's disease - PSP is often confused with PD, but PD does not produce downgaze paresis (Harrison 22e p.3488)
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis / motor neuron disease (FTD-MND overlap) (Harrison 22e p.3486)
nonInfectiousMimics: Psychiatric disease - depression, idiopathic mania, or acting out: the abulia/blandness of frontal degeneration may be misinterpreted as depression and the disinhibition as mania or acting out; FTD can begin with schizophrenia-like features leading to misdiagnosis of a psychiatric condition (Harrison 22e p.3485, p.209)
Other focal frontal lobe causes: head trauma, ruptured aneurysms, hydrocephalus, tumors (metastases, glioblastoma, meningioma) (Harrison 22e p.208)
additionalInvestigations: Structural neuroimaging (MRI) to demonstrate focal frontal/insular/temporal atrophy patterns characteristic of each syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3486)
Genetic testing for C9orf72, GRN, and MAPT mutations in suspected familial cases (Harrison 22e p.3486)
Molecular (tau) PET imaging shows promise but to date binds robustly only to Alzheimer's-related misfolded tau; amyloid PET may help when negative (Harrison 22e p.3487)
redFlags: New-onset disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsivity, or altered dietary preference in a middle-aged adult (Harrison 22e p.3486)
Progressive language breakdown - loss of word/object meaning or inability to produce words (Harrison 22e p.3486)
Emergence of motor neuron disease features in a patient with behavioral or language decline (FTD-MND) (Harrison 22e p.3486)
harrison.prognosis: Caregivers carry a heavy burden, especially as the illness disrupts core emotional and personality functions. There are currently no therapies known to slow progression or improve symptoms; treatment is symptomatic. For the related PSP-RS within the FTD spectrum, death occurs within 5-10 years of onset (Harrison 22e p.3487).
pitfalls: Behavioral variant FTD is frequently mistaken for a primary psychiatric disease - the apathy/blandness can be misread as depression and the disinhibition as mania or acting out; FTD may even begin with schizophrenia-like features and be misdiagnosed as a psychiatric condition. Later age of onset, significant cognitive deficits, or abnormal neuroimaging point to a degenerative process (Harrison 22e p.3485, p.209).
Clinical features do not allow reliable prediction of the underlying FTLD molecular subtype (tau vs TDP-43 vs FET) for all syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3487).
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are largely ineffective in FTD because the cholinergic system is relatively spared, unlike Alzheimer's disease (Harrison 22e p.3486).
Antipsychotics must be used with caution because FTD is often accompanied by parkinsonism, which they can exacerbate (Harrison 22e p.3487).
harrison.severityClassification: No formal severity grading is given; FTD is categorized by core clinical syndrome - behavioral variant (bvFTD), semantic variant PPA, and nonfluent/agrammatic variant PPA - and by underlying FTLD molecular class (FTLD-tau, FTLD-TDP, FTLD-FET) (Harrison 22e p.3486-3487).
management: Symptomatic pharmacotherapy with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors to reduce disinhibition, compulsivity, overeating and other behavioural symptoms of the behavioural variant

Cautious, short-term atypical antipsychotics only for severe agitation or aggression, mindful of extrapyramidal sensitivity, while avoiding cholinesterase inhibitors which are unhelpful and may worsen behaviour
Speech-language therapy and communication strategies for the primary progressive aphasias
Non-pharmacological behavioural management with structured routines and environmental modification
Safety measures addressing impulsivity, driving, financial vulnerability and dysphagia, with dietetic and swallowing assessment
Caregiver education, psychological support and respite given the heavy burden of personality and emotional change
Genetic counselling and testing for C9orf72, GRN and MAPT in familial cases, with cascade testing of relatives
Advance care planning and palliative care as the disease progresses
